variants.title: Run the preparation stages
variants.context: Preparation moves raw observations through five stages. Profile measures schema, missingness, ranges, cardinality, duplicates, event times, and labels. Validate accepts valid records and routes the rest to a reviewable quarantine. Split keeps deployment-time unknowns on the held-out side. Transform fits learned state on training rows and applies it everywhere. Publish versions the partitions with their raw snapshot, code, statistics, checks, and transform artifact.
variants.prompt: A churn dataset is prepared from raw account and billing tables for the first time. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Assign accounts to train, validation, and test so deployment-time unknowns stay on the held-out side.
Measure schema, missingness, ranges, category cardinality, duplicates, event times, and label availability.
Publish the prepared partitions with their raw snapshot, code, schema, statistics, checks, and transform artifact.
Accept records that satisfy the contract and route malformed or impossible ones to a reviewable quarantine.
Fit imputation, scaling, and vocabularies on training rows and apply the frozen state to every other partition.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what the held-out metric is allowed to claim?
variants.explanation: Profile, validate, split, transform, publish. Splitting before fitting is what keeps the evaluation independent of learned state.

variants.prompt: A categorical field starts arriving with values that were never in the vocabulary. Put the stages in order for how the batch is handled.

items.text: Confirm the existing split assignment still holds, since the boundary is defined by entity and time, not by field values.
Check them against the semantic contract and quarantine only the values the vocabulary forbids outright.
Publish the batch with the unknown-value counts recorded alongside its statistics and checks.
Apply the frozen encoder with its declared unknown-category behavior rather than refitting on this batch.
Profile the field and measure how much of the batch carries the unseen values.

variants.hint: Refitting the encoder on the new batch would change the transform mid-release.
variants.explanation: Unknown-category behavior belongs to the frozen transform artifact. Refitting to absorb new values silently changes what the model was trained on.

variants.context: Preparation moves raw observations through five stages. Profile measures schema, missingness, ranges, cardinality, duplicates, event times, and labels. variants.prompt: A source regression is repaired and the affected batch has to be prepared again. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Apply the same versioned transform state rather than refitting on the repaired rows.
Re-run the contract checks so the reconciliation between valid and quarantined counts holds again.
Publish a new immutable dataset version instead of overwriting the one an existing model run used.
Re-profile the repaired input and compare its statistics with the intended baseline.
Reuse the recorded split assignment so the same entities stay on the same side of the boundary.

variants.hint: A repair must not quietly move an entity from test to train.
variants.explanation: Replay is idempotent only when the split assignment and transform state are reused, and the repaired result is a new version.

variants.title: Respond to a preparation alert
variants.context: When a preparation alert fires, identify the first broken boundary and the affected partitions, features, models, and time ranges; stop publication when the contract says the evidence is invalid; preserve the failed candidate, reason counts, snapshot identity, and transform version; repair and replay idempotently; then publish a new immutable version rather than mutating the evidence an existing model run used.
variants.prompt: A duplicate-key alert fires on the nightly orders batch. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Publish a new immutable dataset version and compare its statistics with the intended baseline.
Repair the source or rule and replay the interval idempotently.
Identify the first broken boundary and the partitions, features, models, and time ranges it affects.
Preserve the failed candidate, its reason counts, the raw snapshot identity, and the transform version.
Stop publication so the invalid evidence cannot reach a downstream training job.

variants.hint: A downstream job finishing successfully is not evidence that the data is valid.
variants.explanation: Stop, preserve, repair, republish. Overwriting the failed candidate destroys the evidence the investigation needs.

variants.title: Respond to a preparation alert
variants.context: When a preparation alert fires, identify the first broken boundary and the affected partitions, features, models, and time ranges; stop publication when the contract says the evidence is invalid; preserve the failed candidate, reason counts, snapshot identity, and transform version; repair and replay idempotently; then publish a new immutable version rather than mutating the evidence an existing model run used.
variants.prompt: A field that the contract marks required starts arriving null for one source. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Release the repaired partitions as a new version and leave the failed one intact for review.
Keep the rejected records with reason codes, source identity, and the contract version that rejected them.
Halt publication of those partitions because the structural contract is violated.
Trace the anomaly to the source and the partitions where the required field first went null.
Fix the producer or the contract deliberately, then replay the affected interval.

variants.hint: A required field going null is not the same as a valid null.
variants.explanation: The contract distinguishes a missing required field from a legitimate null, and the reason codes are what make the producer regression diagnosable.

variants.title: Respond to a preparation alert
variants.context: When a preparation alert fires, identify the first broken boundary and the affected partitions, features, models, and time ranges; stop publication when the contract says the evidence is invalid; preserve the failed candidate, reason counts, snapshot identity, and transform version; repair and replay idempotently; then publish a new immutable version rather than mutating the evidence an existing model run used.
variants.prompt: A training-serving skew alert fires: serving missingness for one feature is far above what preparation produced. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Correct the definition or the source and replay the interval through the same versioned transform.
Publish the corrected version and confirm the two paths now agree before retraining.
Hold the next release rather than letting a passing pipeline run mask the mismatch.
Capture the serving statistics, the prepared statistics, and the transform version behind each.
Locate the boundary where the two paths diverge and list the models and time ranges affected.

variants.hint: Investigate skew before retraining on it.
variants.explanation: Retraining on skewed inputs teaches the model the defect. The mismatch is diagnosed and corrected first, then a new version is published.

variants.title: Choose the split boundary
variants.context: The split defines what the held-out metric claims. Use a random or stratified row split only when examples are independent and exchangeable for the deployment question. Use a group-aware split when many rows belong to one customer, patient, device, or document. Use a chronological split when the model predicts a later period from earlier information, and add a gap or embargo when nearby records share delayed labels across the cutoff.
variants.prompt: A demand model predicts next quarter's volume from information available in earlier quarters. Which split matches the deployment question?
options: A stratified random split that balances volume bands across the partitions.
A group-aware split that keeps each product line in a single partition.
A chronological split that trains on earlier periods and evaluates on later ones.
optionFeedback: Random rows put later quarters into training and let the model evaluate on a period it has already seen.
Grouping by product line does not stop future information from reaching the training side.
Correct: the deployment-time unknown is the future, so the held-out side has to be the later period.
variants.hint: What will the model genuinely not know at prediction time?
variants.explanation: The split reproduces the deployment-time unknown. When the unknown is the future, only a chronological boundary can measure it.

variants.title: Choose the split boundary
variants.context: The split defines what the held-out metric claims. Use a random or stratified row split only when examples are independent and exchangeable for the deployment question. Use a group-aware split when many rows belong to one customer, patient, device, or document. Use a chronological split when the model predicts a later period from earlier information, and add a gap or embargo when nearby records share delayed labels across the cutoff.
variants.prompt: A chronological split is in place, but labels for events near the cutoff only settle 14 days later, so records on both sides share the same delayed outcomes. What should be added?
options: A gap or embargo around the cutoff so nearby records cannot share information across it.
A larger test period, so the shared records make up a smaller share of the evaluation.
Stratification by label, so both sides of the cutoff carry the same outcome balance.
optionFeedback: Correct: an embargo removes the window where records on both sides draw on the same delayed labels.
Diluting the contaminated region leaves it in the evaluation and still overstates the score.
Balancing outcomes does nothing about information crossing the cutoff, and it can spread it further.
variants.hint: The cutoff is a line, but the leakage has a width.
variants.explanation: Add a gap when nearby records share delayed labels or aggregates, because a chronological cutoff alone does not separate them.

variants.title: Choose the split boundary
variants.context: The split defines what the held-out metric claims. Use a random or stratified row split only when examples are independent and exchangeable for the deployment question. Use a group-aware split when many rows belong to one customer, patient, device, or document. Use a chronological split when the model predicts a later period from earlier information, and add a gap or embargo when nearby records share delayed labels across the cutoff.
variants.prompt: Each row is one independent inspection with no repeated subject and no time ordering in the deployment question, but only 3 percent of rows are positive. Which split fits?
options: A chronological split using the inspection date as the cutoff.
A stratified row split that preserves the positive rate in every partition.
A group-aware split keyed on the inspector who filed the report.
optionFeedback: A time boundary would measure generalization across periods, which is not the claim being made here.
Correct: the rows are exchangeable for this question, so stratification just stabilizes the rare class across partitions.
Grouping by inspector imposes a boundary the deployment question does not ask for and shrinks the usable data.
variants.hint: Only impose a boundary the deployment question actually needs.
variants.explanation: A random or stratified row split is valid when examples really are independent and exchangeable, and stratification protects a rare class.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity and quality are independent release gates. Effective throughput is workers times observed rows per second per worker times the efficiency factor. Preparation time is input rows divided by effective throughput. Quarantined rows are input rows times the invalid rate, and publishable rows are input rows minus the quarantined rows.
variants.prompt: A batch of 9,000,000 rows runs on 5 workers. Each worker is measured at 2,000 rows per second and the efficiency factor is 0.9. How long does preparation take?
variants.hint: Build the effective throughput before dividing the row count by anything.
variants.explanation: Effective throughput is workers times per-worker throughput times efficiency, and preparation time is input rows divided by that.

mistakes.feedback: Left the efficiency factor out and used the raw 10,000 rows per second.
Used one worker's effective throughput and never multiplied by the worker count.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity and quality are independent release gates. Effective throughput is workers times observed rows per second per worker times the efficiency factor. Preparation time is input rows divided by effective throughput. Quarantined rows are input rows times the invalid rate, and publishable rows are input rows minus the quarantined rows.
variants.prompt: The same batch is re-planned with 8 workers measured at 2,500 rows per second each, at an efficiency factor of 0.8. What is the effective throughput?
variants.hint: Efficiency scales the whole fleet, not one worker's share of it.
variants.explanation: Effective throughput is workers times observed per-worker throughput times efficiency, which is the number every elapsed-time estimate divides by.

mistakes.feedback: Multiplied workers by per-worker throughput and left out the efficiency factor.
Applied the efficiency factor to a single worker and forgot to scale by the worker count.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity and quality are independent release gates. Effective throughput is workers times observed rows per second per worker times the efficiency factor. Preparation time is input rows divided by effective throughput. Quarantined rows are input rows times the invalid rate, and publishable rows are input rows minus the quarantined rows.
variants.prompt: An 8,000,000-row batch has a measured invalid rate of 1.5 percent. Adding workers is already under discussion. How many rows are publishable?
variants.hint: More workers change the elapsed time, not the invalid rate.
variants.explanation: Quarantined rows are input rows times the invalid rate, and publishable rows are what remains, which is a separate gate from finishing on time.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the quarantined count instead of the publishable count.
Added the invalid rows instead of subtracting them.

variants.title: Sort the contract layers
variants.context: A data contract has three parts. The structural contract asks whether the row can be parsed: names, types, required fields, shapes, encodings, and schema compatibility. The semantic contract asks whether the value makes sense: units, ranges, vocabularies, event-time rules, consent, and impossible combinations. The operational contract asks whether the release can be trusted: freshness, completeness, volume, duplicate policy, quarantine limits, and lineage.
variants.prompt: Match each contract layer to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Structural contract
pairs.detail: Names, types, required fields, shapes, valid encodings, and schema compatibility.

pairs.label: Semantic contract
pairs.detail: Units, ranges, category vocabulary, event-time rules, consent, label meaning, and impossible combinations.

pairs.label: Operational contract
pairs.detail: Freshness, completeness, volume, duplicate policy, quarantine limits, lineage, and split policy.

variants.hint: One layer asks whether the row parses, one whether it is believable, one whether the release can ship.
variants.explanation: Keeping the layers separate stops a single quality score from hiding failures that have very different consequences.

variants.prompt: A nightly run produces three findings. Match each finding to the contract layer it belongs to.

pairs.label: A required customer_id field is absent from part of the payload
An order's ship timestamp is earlier than the order timestamp
The newest complete partition is six hours old against a two-hour target

variants.hint: An impossible combination of two valid values is not a parsing failure.
variants.explanation: Each layer names a different owner and repair path, which a generic quality score cannot do.

variants.prompt: A second run produces three findings. Match each finding to the contract layer it belongs to.

pairs.label: A numeric column began arriving as strings after a producer change
Weights are recorded in pounds where the contract declares kilograms
Quarantine volume has passed the limit the release policy allows

variants.hint: A value can parse perfectly and still mean the wrong thing.
variants.explanation: Units belong to the semantic contract, while a quarantine limit is an operational statement about whether the release can be trusted.
